nameStory: This beetle's species name 'cyanescens' comes from the Greek word for blue-green, describing its metallic sheen that can shift from deep blue to greenish tones depending on the light. Like other jewel beetles, it earned its family name from the brilliant, gem-like colors that make these insects look like tiny living jewels crawling on tree bark.
description: The Blue-green Jewel Beetle is a small, metallic wood-boring beetle that shimmers with blue-green iridescence. These slender beetles typically measure about a quarter to half-inch long and have an elongated, streamlined body shape. Adults are most commonly seen on sunny days crawling on tree bark or flying between host trees. As wood-borers, their larvae develop inside tree branches and stems, creating tunnels as they feed.

idTips.label: Metallic Blue-Green Color
idTips.description: The most striking feature is the brilliant metallic blue-green sheen that shifts colors as the beetle moves in sunlight, feeling smooth and hard like polished metal when touched

idTips.label: Elongated Body Shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly narrow and torpedo-shaped, roughly three times longer than wide, giving it a streamlined appearance unlike rounder beetles

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Typically measures 6-12mm (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch) long, small enough to easily fit on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Hard Wing Covers
idTips.description: Wing covers (elytra) feel extremely hard and rigid when gently touched, making a tiny tapping sound if brushed with a fingernail

idTips.label: Antennae Shape
idTips.description: Short, slightly serrated antennae that look like tiny saws, quite different from the long, thread-like antennae of longhorn beetles

habitat: Found in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, particularly where birch, maple, and oak trees are present. Adults are most often spotted on sun-warmed bark of dead or stressed trees, fence posts, or recently cut wood. They prefer forest edges and clearings where sunlight can reach the tree trunks, as they're attracted to warm, sunny spots.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from overwintering sites in late spring, becoming active on warm, sunny days above 65°F. Look for them crawling on bark or flying short distances between trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen mating and laying eggs. They're most active during the hottest part of sunny days, often resting motionless on bark during cooler morning hours.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity decreases as temperatures drop, though they may still be seen on unusually warm autumn days. This is when larvae are actively boring through wood, though they're hidden from view.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in bark crevices and wood debris. Larvae continue developing slowly inside host trees, creating tiny sawdust piles at tunnel entrances that may be visible on snow.

funFact: When threatened, jewel beetles can 'play dead' so convincingly that they remain completely motionless for several minutes, but here's the amazing part: they can actually survive being pinned in insect collections for hours and then fly away when released, leading to many surprised entomologists finding empty pins in their collection boxes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the invasive Emerald Ash Borer, which has a similar metallic green color but is slightly larger and more emerald-green rather than blue-green. Memory trick: 'Cyanescens has more Cyan (blue) in its color' - if you see more blue tones, it's likely the native Blue-green Jewel Beetle rather than the invasive Emerald Ash Borer.
contextualKnowledge: Unlike the notorious Emerald Ash Borer that has devastated ash trees across North America, this native jewel beetle is generally not considered a serious forest pest. However, all Agrilus beetles can be challenging for non-experts to distinguish, so any metallic green beetle found on ash trees should be reported to local extension offices for proper identification.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, the Blue-green Jewel Beetle is distinguished by its blue-green coloration versus the Red-necked Cane Borer's reddish neck area and the Emerald Ash Borer's brighter emerald-green color. It's also typically smaller than the Emerald Ash Borer and attacks a wider variety of tree species rather than specializing on ash trees like its infamous cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its notorious relative the Emerald Ash Borer which is uniformly bright green and attacks ash trees, the red-necked cane borer has that distinctive reddish thorax and targets berry canes.

Unlike its relatives the red-necked cane borer (which attacks berry canes and has a reddish thorax) and other Agrilus species that often have bronze or copper coloring, emerald ash borer is distinctly emerald green all over.
